# The world of Veyra

Everything a new Keeper knows on the first evening, then the lore found later in the year (marked with when it is found).

## The River Lethe

The Lethe rises far inland, in the high bogs of the Morrowfen, where no birds sing and the water is the colour of old pewter. It runs two hundred miles to the Grey Sea, and for the last nine of those miles it runs past Veyra.

Every evening, as the light goes, a silver mist lifts off the river and climbs the streets of the city. The old folk call it the Tide. It is cool and soft and smells faintly of rain on stone, and it is the most dangerous thing in the world. Whatever a person is not holding firmly in mind when the Tide passes over them, it takes. A name half-remembered. A recipe never quite learned. The face of a friend not seen in years.

Most nights the Tide is thin and takes only small things. Some nights it is thick, and takes a great deal.

## The Lamp-Wardens and the Compact

Nine hundred years ago, in the time the songs call the Drowned Years, the river-folk who lived along the Lethe forgot everything: their names, their gods, the way home. They lived like sleepwalkers, and their kings are remembered only as the Nameless Kings, because no one could recall what they had been called.

Then came Ysolde of the Lamp, the first Warden. She had learned, no one knows from whom, that a mind which sets its memories in places, room by room, stone by stone, can stand in the Tide and lose nothing. She taught the Art to twelve others. Together they swore the Compact of Lamps: to build a city that was itself a memory, and to keep a lamp burning in it for every person who chose to remember.

That city was Veyra. Its twelve districts are twelve great routes, laid out by the Wardens so that anyone who walked them could store their life along the way.

## The Art of Places

The Wardens called their method the Art of Places. You will know it by other names: the Memory Palace, the Journey, the Method of Loci. It is very old, older than Veyra, and it is not magic, though in Veyra it is treated with the respect usually given to magic.

The idea is simple enough to explain to a child. Choose a place you know well. Walk through it in your mind, stopping at the same spots in the same order. At each stop, leave a picture of the thing you wish to keep, and make the picture do something to the place. Later, walk the route again, and the pictures will be waiting.

In Veyra it is said that a Warden at the height of the Art could walk through a Tide as thick as wool and come out the other side still knowing the name of every person they had ever met.

## The Long Quiet

For six hundred years the Wardens kept the Compact. Then, slowly, they stopped needing to. The Archive filled with ledgers. Paper was cheaper than practice. Why train for years to hold a memory when you could write it down and put it on a shelf?

The lamps went out one at a time, the way the stars go in the morning: not all at once, but so gradually that no one could say which night the sky turned grey. By the time of this story there were no Wardens left, only the Archivist and a handful of clerks, and the city trusted its ledgers completely.

This is the age the songs call the Long Quiet. It ended on the night the Tide rose higher than it had in three hundred years, and every ledger in the Archive came back blank.

# Lore found during the year

> **Spoilers.** This page reveals the story as it unfolds through the year. Read the world and district pages first if you want to discover it in the game.

## The Forgettings

*Found after the Lamplighters' Quay is restored (month 1).*

When the Tide loosens a memory, it does not destroy it. The memory drifts down into the streets and settles as a small grey shape, soft at the edges, like dust in a sunbeam. The old folk call these shapes Forgettings. They are not evil, and they have never hurt anyone. A Forgetting is simply what the Tide leaves behind.

Each one holds the lost thing carefully and waits to be remembered, rather like a shy dog that has wandered far from home. A Keeper does not drive a Forgetting away. A Keeper remembers the thing properly, and the grey shape grows light, sighs, and goes home. The Wardens called this an Echo, because the memory answers when it is called.

Forgettings come in kinds that match what was lost. Pictures leave a Smudge, stories a Tangle, places a Hollow, faces a Blank, numbers some Static, words a Murmur, and facts a Dustleaf. The oldest and largest of them, the Great Forgetting, is only the forgotten things of the whole city, gathered in one place and very tired.

## The Archive and the Ledgers

*Found after the Lamplighters' Quay is restored (month 1).*

The Archive crowns the highest tier of Veyra: a round hall of pale stone under a dome of green copper, with bronze doors that are never fully closed. Its shelves climb in rings to the roof, and on them stand the Ledgers, one for every year since the founding.

At the centre of the floor stands the Lamp of Ysolde, a great bowl of brass on a pillar of black stone. It has not been lit in living memory. The clerks dust it on the first day of every month out of habit, and nobody knows why.

It was believed that ink could not be touched by the Tide. The night Calder vanished proved otherwise. The Tide did not reach the Ledgers. Something else did.

## Lethewater, or "the Grey"

*Found after the The Long Gallery is restored (month 2).*

If you boil the river water in copper and catch the steam in glass, you get a few drops of a clear, faintly silver liquid that smells of nothing. The dock folk call it the grey. A single drop on the tongue will take away one memory, if you hold that memory in mind as you swallow. A spoonful will take a year. A cup will take a life.

For most of the city's history the grey was forbidden. In the Long Quiet it became merely discouraged, then tolerated, then sold. Widows bought it to forget their grief. Soldiers bought it to forget the war. The rich bought it to forget their debts, and the poor bought it to forget they were hungry.

The trade is run by the Salt Guild, who distil it in the marsh-houses south of the city. It has made them very rich. It has made Veyra very quiet.

## The Salt Guild

*Found after the The Counting House is restored (month 4).*

On paper the Salt Guild trades in salt, which it rakes from the pans at the river mouth. In truth salt is a cover for the grey, and has been for forty years.

The Guild's masters wear white gloves and never touch the stuff themselves. They keep their books in a number code that changes every season. In Calder's ledgers, decoded, you found the same entry repeated every month for nine years: a large payment from the Salt Guild to an account marked only with a closed eye.

The closed eye is the sign of the Quiet Order.

## The Quiet Order

*Found after the The Hall of Faces is restored (month 3).*

They wear hooded robes the colour of river mist, and they speak softly, and they are very kind. They run soup kitchens on the Quay and sit with the dying in the Lower Tiers. They call themselves the Hushed.

Their teaching is gentle, and it is this: that memory is the root of all suffering. That every grief, every grudge, every war began with someone who could not forget. That the Tide is not a curse but a mercy, and the Wardens were wrong to fight it.

Their leader is called the Grand Hush. Few have seen his face. Those who have say that he has the kindest eyes they have ever seen, and that he looks at you as if he already forgives you for something you have not done yet.

## The Night of No Moon

*Found after the The Clockwork Market is restored (month 5).*

Once in every nineteen years, the dark of the moon falls on the longest night of winter. On that night the Lethe runs at its highest, and the Tide that rises from it is not a mist but a wall.

In the old days the Wardens stood on the Lethe Gate, the great sluice-works at the head of the city, and held the floodgates shut by hand while the whole city stood in the streets with lamps and sang the old songs until dawn. It was called the Long Vigil.

The next Night of No Moon falls this winter. Calder's last ledger entry, the unfinished sum, was the date of it.

## The Ammerhold and the Outer Roads

*Found after the The Mirror Wards is restored (month 9).*

Veyra is built into the seaward face of the Ammerhold, a long ridge of grey granite that runs from the mountains to the coast like the spine of some buried beast. Behind it lie the Outer Roads: a web of old trade-ways linking a hundred small towns, most of which have never seen the Tide.

Road-wardens keep those ways. They are a rough, independent people who walk everywhere, own very little, and owe loyalty to no lord. They are hard to frighten and impossible to bribe, which is why the Salt Guild has always hated them.

## The Hollow Villages

*Found after the The Open Roads is restored (month 10).*

On the Outer Roads there are towns where the grey arrived before the Tide ever could. Barrowmere. Stillwater. Fenwick Cross. The Salt Guild sold to them first, cheaply, as a cure for sorrow.

Now the people of those towns smile at strangers and have no idea how long they have lived there. Their fields go half-planted because no one remembers what was sown. Their children are not taught to read, because who would remember to teach them? They are not unhappy. That is the most frightening part.

## The Rite of Echoes

*Found after the The Amphitheatre of Echoes is restored (month 11).*

By ancient law any citizen may challenge the keeper of an office to the Rite of Echoes: a contest of memory held in the great Amphitheatre before the whole city. Words, numbers, faces, tongues and histories, each in turn, until one contestant falters.

The winner holds the office. The loser drinks a cup of the grey, before everyone, and forgets that they ever held it. The Rite has not been called in two hundred years.

## The Heartledger

*Found after the The Lethe Gate is restored (month 12).*

Every Ledger in the Archive is a copy. The Wardens kept one original record of the city, the Heartledger, which held the true names, the true histories and the true promises of Veyra. Without it, the Compact of Lamps is only a story.

The Heartledger was never written on paper. It was kept the old way, in the mind of each Archivist in turn, walked and re-walked along a palace route that ran through all twelve districts. When an Archivist died, the next one had already learned the route.

On the night of the great Tide, Calder did not have a successor ready. So she chose one. She chose you.

## The Lamplighter's Song

*Found after the side quest "Tansy's Remembering Tea".*

Sung on the Quay at dusk when the lamps are lit. Tansy says it is older than the city.

> When grey comes up from Lethe's bed
> and takes the names from all our dead,
> then light the lamp and walk the hall,
> and set a picture by each wall.
> What you have placed you shall not lose,
> though the grey take all it choose.
> So walk the road and light the way
> and keep your night until it's day.

## The Brothers Hask

*Found after the side quest "The Drifter's Brother".*

There were two of them, Joss and Tomas Hask, road-wardens out of Kettering Ford. Tomas was the talker. Joss was the one who listened.

Two years ago Tomas followed a Salt Guild wagon into the marsh-houses and did not come out. When Joss found him a month later, in a hollow village on the Outer Roads, Tomas smiled at him politely and asked if he was lost.

Joss Hask has been walking toward Veyra ever since.

## House Varre

*Found after the side quest "Isolde's Invitation".*

The Varres have held the office of Harbour Mistress for eleven generations, and in all that time no ship has docked in Veyra without paying them, and no secret has crossed the Grey Sea without being sold to them first.

They are said to keep their own ledgers, in their own heads, by an art older than the Wardens' and less honest. Isolde Varre is the last of them, and the most dangerous.

## The Unnamed

*Found after passing "The Catacombs of the Unnamed".*

The statues under the Hall of Faces were carved in the Drowned Years by a mason who could no longer remember her own children's names. She carved their faces so she could at least keep those.

The Wardens later added a plaque to every statue and a logbook beside the lectern. The plaques wore away. The logbook did not, because somebody always came down to read it.

## The Drain Chain

*Found after passing "The Sunken Scriptorium".*

The Scriptorium floods every few years. The scribes of old fitted a great iron drain under the lower floor and hid its chain behind the map table, so that only someone who knew the room by heart could find it in grey water.

## The Salt Guild Code

*Found after passing "The Broken Vault of the Salt Guild".*

The Salt Guild changed its vault code every night and wrote it in a single ledger. Its clerks were not allowed to copy it. They had to carry it home in their heads, as pictures along the walk from the cellar to their door.

## The Gargoyles of the Bridge

*Found after passing "The Bridge of Tongues".*

The gargoyles of the Tongues Bridge were carved in the year 333 to keep the old tongue alive. They do not care how quickly a traveller learns. They only ask whether the words are still there a week later.

## The Market Clock

*Found after passing "The Disordered Gears".*

The great clock of the Clockwork Market has stopped four times in its history. Each time, the stallholders put it back together from memory, walking the square from the tower steps back to the tea urn.

## The Brass Years

*Found after passing "The Hall of Years".*

The Hall of Years was lined with brass labels, one for each year the Wardens thought worth keeping. The Tide rubbed the numbers off, and the events carved above them stayed. A scholar who knows the events can put the years back, one frame at a time.

## The Reckoning Table

*Found after passing "The Counting House Reckoning".*

The old merchants of the Counting House worked their sums aloud and left nothing on paper. They said each step as they went, so that a sum was only ever as long as a breath. Isolde keeps the tally stick from the table drawer on her desk, and says every notch is a sum somebody got right.

## The Sealed Vaults

*Found after passing "The Quay Vault".*

The Wardens hid small vaults all over Veyra, each with a tablet beside its door. A vault opens only for someone who can say its tablet back after a long wait. The Wardens thought this was fair: anyone may read a tablet, but only someone who keeps it may open the door.

## The Keeper's Ledger

*Found after the Lamplighters' Quay is restored (month 1).*

On the night of the great Tide every ledger in the Archive came back blank. Nine hundred years of sums and names went white as milk in a single hour.

Calder kept one of the blank books. He gives it to each new Keeper after the Gallery gate, with one rule: the book only tells you what to ask yourself. Each book a Keeper starts becomes a spine on the shelf of the Long Gallery, and a spine glows warmer as its cards are kept.

## Old Echoes

*Found after the The Long Gallery is restored (month 2).*

Most Forgettings are young and quick. A few are old: they sank to the bottom of the Undercroft a season ago and have been climbing back up ever since, slow and faint, carrying something a Keeper learned long before.

They come to the Long Vigil as Old Echoes. Hold what one carries and a lamp on the battlements stays lit until the season turns.

## The Evening Round

*Found after the The Scriptorium is restored (month 7).*

The Lamplighter's Song is sung on the Quay every dusk, and nobody on the Quay has forgotten a verse of it in nine hundred years. Tansy says the secret is not in the singing but in the order: a little of it every night, round and round, so no verse ever has time to slip.

Keepers keep their own long texts the same way. Each evening one portion is the lamplighters' verse of the night.

## The Gloss

*Found after the The Scriptorium is restored (month 7).*

When the scribes' two chronicles disagreed, Brother Ennick found the false one by its margins. A scribe who truly knows a passage can write a gloss beside it: its meaning, in plain words. The false chronicle's glosses did not match its text.

Writing a gloss became a Scriptorium habit. Ennick keeps a row of yours on his desk. "Fewer mistakes than last month. I am writing that down too."

## The Merchants' Marks

*Found after the The Counting House is restored (month 4).*

The Salt Guild's merchants worked their sums aloud at the Reckoning Table, and they had a picture for every mark: a pair of scales for equals, a gull with spread wings for more, a cut rope for less, a loaf broken in two for share, a vine for grows by.

Isolde still teaches them. Calder's last entry in the Ledger of Debts stopped in the middle of a sum. A Keeper who learns the Marks can finish it.

## The Turning Stones

*Found after the The Tongues Bridge is restored (month 6).*

On the Tongues Bridge some paving stones turn underfoot. Each shows a different face as it turns: I, you, she, we, they. The gargoyles let a traveller over only when the traveller names the right face for the stone.

The old tongue changes its words the same way. Keepers call the changing words turning stones, and the bridge's lanterns, two and later three, are how they remember which family a word belongs to.

## The Joke Box

*Found after the The Hall of Faces is restored (month 3).*

Tansy's tea room keeps a battered box of jokes that the Quay folk swap on Vigil nights to stay awake. It is sorted by topic, a little drawer for each, like a very small palace.

The rule of the box: you only need to keep the key word. The rest of the joke comes back on its own.

## The Travellers' Satchel

*Found after the The Open Roads is restored (month 10).*

Travellers on the Open Roads bring books from outside Veyra. Few can carry a whole book in their heads, so they carry a satchel of ideas instead: one idea from each chapter, in their own words, asked again until it stays.

## The Wardens' Road

*Found after the The Clockwork Market is restored (month 5).*

Veyra once had thirteen Lamp-Wardens, and the Wardens did not stop at twelve routes. Each kept a discipline of the Art, numbers or cards or faces or the hours, and wrote it on a tablet. When the Tide came the tablets were scattered through the Undercroft and the sealed vaults.

Walking the Wardens' Road means learning each lost Warden's discipline from their tablet. It is a long road, and a hobby road: the old Wardens practised for years. Ottoline Gilt is on it too, and her marks keep following yours.

## The Quay Lamps

*Found after the The Clockwork Market is restored (month 5).*

Before the clocks, the Quay signalled the height of the Tide with its lamps, lit or dark, in rows of three. Every lamp-boy could read a row at a glance: dark, lit, lit was three; lit, lit, lit was seven. The Wardens kept long strings of these rows in their heads, and that is the Binary discipline.

## The Players of the Clockwork Market

*Found after the The Clockwork Market is restored (month 5).*

Once a year the Clockwork Market performed the Tide schedule as a pageant with a hundred Players, one for each number from 00 to 99. Each Player had a costume, a deed and a prop, and three numbers in a row became one short scene: this Player, doing that Player's deed, with the third Player's prop.

The Players are long gone. A Keeper on the Wardens' Road casts a new hundred of their own.

## Ennick's Book of Slips

*Found after the The Clockwork Market is restored (month 5).*

Brother Ennick writes down every mistake he makes, with the date, in a small brown book. He says it is the most useful book in the Scriptorium, because it tells him exactly what to practise next.

A Keeper on the Wardens' Road keeps one too. Ennick is still writing his own mistakes down. Fewer of them.

## Tallow's Hours

*Found after the The Lethe Gate is restored (month 12).*

Ambrose Tallow wound the Mother Clock, and it ticks one number a second. The Warden of the Hours kept an hour nobody wrote down: an hour of numbers, an hour of cards, an hour of listening to the clock and keeping the count.

Few Keepers ever walk Tallow's Hours. Those who do say the hour itself is the easy part. The years before it are the work.

## A Ring With One Hand

*Found after the Lamplighters' Quay is restored (month 1).*

Under the rust at the foot of the last lamp on the Quay, someone long ago worked a small mark into the iron: a ring with a single hand inside it, like a clock with nothing to say.

Tansy says the lamplighters call it the winding mark, and rub it for luck on their way past. She does not know who made it. She rubs it anyway.

## The Hour Nobody Wrote

*Found after the The Clockwork Market is restored (month 5).*

The Wardens' timetable for the Tide runs for nineteen years, every night of it, and there is no entry for nine minutes past eleven on the night of the great Tide. It simply is not there. The clocks stopped on a minute the Wardens never planned for.

On the back plate of the Mother Clock is the ring with one hand. The winding key was left in the lock, and when you put your palm on it, it was warm.

## The Oldest Stone

*Found after the The Tongues Bridge is restored (month 6).*

At the foot of the Tongues Bridge, below the waterline in a dry summer, is a block older than the rest. Beside it, cut small, is the ring with one hand, and one word of the old tongue. You can read it now. It says: Wait.

Wren says it might be a builder's note. She says it quickly, and does not look at the stone again.

## Someone Is Very Fond of Us

*Found after the The Mirror Wards is restored (month 9).*

In the Order's record room there is a standing order that has never been cancelled: oil for the lamps and wicks for the lamps, paid every month for eleven years from a purse stamped with a ring and a single hand. Nobody in the Order has ever met the person who pays.

"Someone is very fond of us," Ennick said, and then, because he had been practising, he said what he actually thought: "I do not like it. A gift that never asks for anything is a kind of asking."

## The Seam

*Found when the Keeper first meets the Great Forgetting (Chapter 13).*

Under the Undercroft, below the Last Stone, is the place where the Lethe truly rises. The Wardens never named it. Wren calls it the Seam, because it is where two edges of time were sewn badly and have been pulling at each other ever since.

The Seam takes nothing away. It only tangles. A thing that is forgotten is gone, and the person is calm about it. A thing that is tangled is known but in the wrong place: loaves baked for the wrong day, one dog with three names, two brothers who each remember the other in a different year.

The Seam cannot be closed by force, or by wishing, or by forgetting more. It can only be stitched, by remembering things in their true order. It gives back the days it snagged. It does not undo what the river takes in the ordinary way, and it does not undo what anyone chose to let go. The Tide still rises every evening. That is the river being the river.

## The Great Forgetting

*Found when the Seam is closed (Chapter 13).*

The old songs say that every lost thing in Veyra went somewhere, and that for nine hundred years they all went to the same place. The Quay folk say that on the highest tide of the year you can see it: a giant of grey mist with a pale glow for a face, standing on the Lethe.

What the songs did not know is that the giant was not made of lost things alone. It was made of days that had been tangled out of order on a thread, and held there by one lonely man who could not bear to let an evening end.

The Wardens never fought it. They had a different idea. They said that the way to deal with a very large Forgetting is the way to deal with a very small one: say the thing back, kindly, one piece at a time, until it can rest. It turns out that the same is true of a Warden.

## The Part the Quay Folk Only Hum

*Found after Wren's story beat "The third verse".*

The Lamplighter's Song has a third verse that people mostly hum. Tansy says it is the part for the very end of the evening.

> Trim the wick and turn the key,
> Tallow keeps the lamp for me.
> By river stones and light, go home:
> the last lamp waits, and none walk alone.

Everyone on the Quay took "Tallow" to mean candle fat. Wren says her mother never said otherwise.

## What Was Kept for Her Face

*Found once the four details of Wren's mother's face are kept.*

You have kept four things about Marit Halloway's face for Wren: the scar through the left eyebrow, the brass key in her hair, the yellow scarf and the laugh that began before the joke was over.

Wren says she turns them over in the evenings like coins. "I still cannot see her. But I can see where she would be standing. That is something. That is a great deal."

## The Last Lamp, Kept

*Found once the tune and the lamps are kept.*

You kept the tune. You also kept what Marit was doing while she hummed it: lighting the lamps along the Quay, one to twenty-two.

Wren hummed it for you on the stairs of the Archive, once, all the way through. The lamp in the stairwell brightened a little, which Tansy says lamps do not do. Wren says they do for her.

## Wren's Keepsakes

*Found once the Keeper has kept a detail from Wren's story.*

Small things Wren asks about once they have been kept: the stirs of her tea, the colour of the door, the name of her cat, the scar through her mother's eyebrow. Each held detail is kept here as a warm line from Wren. (This entry grows as the Keeper plays.)
